text: Reinhold Rudenberg (or Rüdenberg) was a German-American electrical engineer and inventor recognized for numerous innovations in electric power and related fields, including improvements in large alternating current generators, the electrostatic-lens electron microscope, carrier-current communications on power lines, a form of phased array radar, an explanation of power blackouts, preferred number series, and the number prefix "Giga-". Born in Hannover to a Jewish family, he had a father, Georg, who ran a plant for preparing and cleaning feathers and down, and a mother who was the daughter of the Chief Rabbi of Braunschweig. He studied at Leibniz University Hannover (then Technische Hochschule), earning both his electrical engineering degree (Dipl. Ing.) and doctorate (Dr. Ing.) in 1906. He worked as a teaching assistant for Professor Ludwig Prandtl at Göttingen University, where he also took courses in physics and the Advanced Electrodynamics course taught by Emil Wiechert, a former discoverer of the electron. In 1919, he married Lily Minkowski, daughter of Hermann Minkowski and Auguste née Adler; their son, H. Gunther Rudenberg, was born from this marriage. Rudenberg taught at Göttingen, Berlin, London, and in the United States at MIT and Harvard University, serving as head of the Department of Electrical Engineering at Harvard’s Graduate School of Engineering from 1939 to 1952, when he retired. After leaving Göttingen in 1908, he joined Siemens-Schuckertwerke (SSW), a Siemens company in Berlin, starting as a machine design engineer and quickly advancing to head the machine design department. His work expanded to include transmission lines, distribution systems, and protective relays and switches. In 1923, he was appointed Director of the Scientific Department (Wissenschaftliche Abteilung) of SSW and named Chief Electrical Engineer (Chef-Elektriker) of the firm. In 1916, he designed the electric generator for the main power station in Cologne, which was then the largest known. He was a prolific inventor and author, with his books on electrical transients widely used as college texts. In 1930, shortly after returning from a summer vacation in the Netherlands, his 2 3⁄4-year-old son fell ill with poliomyelitis, a disease with a 10–25% death rate that affected the legs and could progress to the lungs; at the time, the virus was known to be too small to be seen under an optical microscope. Determined to visualize such small particles, Rudenberg, inspired by his studies of electrons under Wiechert’s guidance, believed electrons could resolve virus particles and began investigating methods to focus them to create enlarged images. In 1927, Hans Busch, a friend from Göttingen, had published an analysis of a magnetic coil acting as a lens. Rudenberg reasoned that an electron beam from a point on an object in an axially symmetric electrostatic system could be focused back to an image point if the radial electric field was proportional to the electron’s distance from the axis, enabling real magnified images. As a public lecture on electron optics approached, Siemens applied for a patent on Rudenberg’s electrostatic-lens instrument and general electron microscope principles on May 30, 1931, securing patents in six other countries. Germany later granted patents on this or related inventions between 1938 and 1954. Some competitors raised objections to the Rudenberg patents but failed to acknowledge that he began his work in 1930, the specific stimulus that prompted it, or the technical differences between his electrostatic lenses and the magnetic lenses used by others.
